introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah sees God gathering people of every nation and language to see his glory. In the Gospel, someone asks Jesus whether only a few will be saved, and he answers, Strive to enter through the narrow door; people will come from east and west to the feast in God's Kingdom. The Letter to the Hebrews tells us that the Lord disciplines those he loves. Let us strive to enter by the narrow door.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord's faithfulness endures forever. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may welcome people from every nation into the Kingdom of God. Let us pray to the Lord.
For missionaries who carry God's glory to distant lands: that their words may bear fruit. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are going through hard times: that they may trust that God trains and loves them as his children. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who think faith can be taken for granted: that they may strive to enter by the narrow door. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may lift up our drooping hands and weak knees and walk the straight path. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you call people from every nation to the feast of your Kingdom. Give us the strength to enter by the narrow door, and bring us to sit at your table. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The narrow door
reflection.body:
At the end of the Book of Isaiah, God announces a vision as wide as the world: "The time comes that I will gather all nations and languages, and they will come, and will see my glory." Messengers will go to distant islands "who have not heard my fame," and people of every nation will come to God's holy mountain. The shortest psalm in the Bible answers: "Praise the LORD, all you nations!"

In the Gospel, as Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, someone asks him, "Lord, are they few who are saved?" Jesus does not give a number. He gives an urgent call: "Strive to enter in by the narrow door." Salvation is God's gift, but it is not automatic. It asks for a real response.

Jesus warns that knowing about him is not enough. Some will say, "We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets." But the master will say, "I don't know where you come from." Being near Jesus is different from following him.

Then comes the wide vision again: "They will come from the east, west, north, and south, and will sit down in God's Kingdom." And a reversal: "there are some who are last who will be first, and there are some who are first who will be last." No one should be complacent, and no one should give up hope.

The Letter to the Hebrews helps us understand our struggles. God treats us as his children, and "whom the Lord loves, he disciplines." Discipline is not pleasant at the time, "yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness." So, "lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees."

This week, ask yourself whether you are only near Jesus, or really following him. Take one concrete step through the narrow door: a habit to change, a person to forgive, a prayer to begin.
